subject: Anthropology
title: The First Cities
description: A 60-second lesson on The First Cities.

hook.text: Uruk had 40,000 people by 3000 BCE — temples, markets, workshops, and streets. The city was born in Mesopotamia.

buildup.text: The first cities arose in river valleys: Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus, and China, where irrigation fed large groups.

discovery.text: Cities concentrated people, creating specialization — priests, potters, scribes, and soldiers living side by side.

twist.text: Cities also created inequality, disease, and waste. Dense living brought problems that villages never faced.

climax.text: The first cities were experiments in living together at scale. Their solutions — and failures — still echo today.

quiz.question: Where did the first cities arise?
options: In river valleys with irrigation potential

details.summary: The first cities emerged around 3500 BCE in Mesopotamia, followed by urban centers in Egypt, the Indus Valley, and China. Urbanization concentrated populations, specialized labor, created bureaucracies, and produced the social complexity we associate with civilization.
details.whyItMatters: Cities changed everything about human social organization. Understanding how and why urbanization occurred reveals the origins of government, writing, taxation, and social classes that still structure our world today.
takeaways: The first cities appeared around 3500 BCE in Mesopotamia
Urbanization concentrated population and specialized labor
Cities produced bureaucracy, writing, taxation, and social hierarchy

faq.question: What makes a settlement qualify as a city?
faq.answer: Archaeologists look for large populations, occupational specialization beyond farming, monumental architecture, social stratification, administrative systems, and long-distance trade. Not all criteria need be present, and definitions vary among scholars.

faq.question: Did cities develop independently in different regions?
faq.answer: Yes. Mesopotamian, Egyptian, Indus Valley, Chinese, Mesoamerican, and Andean cities developed largely independently. This convergence suggests that urbanization responds to common pressures like population growth, agricultural surplus, and the need for coordination.
